overview: Both are workhorse diagnostic techniques, but they detect fundamentally different kinds of evidence of infection or exposure.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: An immunoassay that uses antibody-antigen binding and an enzyme-linked colorimetric or fluorescent readout to detect or quantify a protein, antigen, or antibody in a sample.
aspects.valueB: A molecular technique that exponentially amplifies a specific DNA (or reverse-transcribed RNA) sequence so it becomes detectable, using repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension.

aspects.label: Target
aspects.valueA: Protein: an antigen or an antibody raised against one.
aspects.valueB: Nucleic acid: a specific DNA sequence (or RNA, via RT-PCR).

aspects.label: Specimen
aspects.valueA: Serum, plasma, or other fluids containing the target protein/antibody.
aspects.valueB: Any specimen yielding intact nucleic acid — blood, swabs, tissue, CSF, etc.

aspects.label: Key Reagents
aspects.valueA: Capture/detection antibodies, enzyme conjugate (e.g. HRP), chromogenic or fluorescent substrate.
aspects.valueB: Sequence-specific primers, thermostable DNA polymerase (e.g. Taq), dNTPs, buffer with Mg2+.

aspects.label: Detection / Readout
aspects.valueA: Colorimetric or fluorescent signal, read by spectrophotometry (optical density).
aspects.valueB: Amplicon visualized by gel electrophoresis (conventional PCR) or fluorescence accumulated in real time (qPCR).

aspects.label: Sensitivity
aspects.valueA: Good, but generally lower than PCR — depends on antigen/antibody concentration reaching a detectable threshold.
aspects.valueB: Very high — can, in principle, detect a single copy of target sequence after sufficient amplification cycles.

aspects.label: Time Required
aspects.valueA: Typically a few hours, including incubation and wash steps.
aspects.valueB: Roughly one to a few hours for amplification, plus extraction time; results can be same-day.

aspects.label: Controls
aspects.valueA: Positive/negative controls and a standard curve for quantitative ELISA.
aspects.valueB: Positive, negative (no-template), and often an internal amplification control.

aspects.label: Interpretation
aspects.valueA: Optical density above/below a cutoff determines reactive vs non-reactive; useful for exposure/seroconversion status.
aspects.valueB: Presence/absence (or cycle threshold, Ct, in qPCR) indicates presence and relative quantity of the target sequence — useful for active infection.

aspects.label: Common Artifacts
aspects.valueA: Cross-reactivity causing false positives; the 'window period' before antibodies develop causing false negatives.
aspects.valueB: Contamination causing false positives; PCR inhibitors in the sample causing false negatives.

aspects.label: Limitations / Pitfalls
aspects.valueA: Detects immune response or antigen presence, not necessarily viable/active infection; window period limits early detection.
aspects.valueB: Detects genetic material, which can persist after an organism is no longer viable/infectious; requires intact nucleic acid and proper primer design.

aspects.label: When to Choose
aspects.valueA: Screening for past exposure or immune status, high-throughput serosurveys.
aspects.valueB: Confirming active infection, detecting very low pathogen loads, or when a specific genetic sequence itself is the question.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Measures the immune/antigen picture via antibody binding.
aspects.valueB: Measures the genetic picture via sequence amplification.

aspects.label: Primary Purpose / Indication
aspects.valueA: Detecting or quantifying a specific antigen or antibody — often used for exposure/immunity screening.
aspects.valueB: Detecting or quantifying a specific nucleic acid sequence — often used to confirm active infection or genetic identity.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: If a question says 'antigen-antibody binding with a color change,' think ELISA. If it says 'amplifying DNA/RNA,' think PCR.
overlay.memoryTrick: ELISA = proteins and antibodies. PCR = pieces of the genome, photocopied.
overlay.choiceRule: Ask: am I looking for evidence the immune system reacted (ELISA), or evidence the organism's genetic material is physically present (PCR)?
overlay.commonMisconception: A positive PCR does not always mean an actively infectious organism — it means the target sequence was present in detectable amounts.
